title: Tea Leaves

seo.title: Tea Leaves (Camellia sinensis, Chai Patti) - Benefits, Uses and Safety
seo.description: Learn about tea leaves, including botanical identity, Ayurvedic qualities, traditional kitchen uses, caffeine considerations, dosage and safety.

short_description: Tea leaves are the dried leaves of Camellia sinensis, a bitter-astringent, heating kitchen infusion used for alertness and light Kapha, but drying and stimulating if overused.
full_description:
Tea leaves are the processed leaves of Camellia sinensis, known in Hindi as chai patti. Tea is not a classical Charaka-era dravya; it entered Indian kitchen use later. In contemporary Ayurvedic reading it is tikta and kashaya (bitter and astringent), laghu and ruksha (light and dry), and ushna (heating), with a stimulating effect from caffeine.

A modest cup may feel clearing for Kapha and helpful after a heavy meal. Excess tea commonly aggravates Pitta (acidity, heat, restlessness) and Vata (dryness, insomnia, jitteriness). It is not a substitute for tulsi or ginger tea in cough care. Prefer a light infusion rather than a long, strong decoction, and avoid it on an empty stomach if you have reflux or feel ungrounded.

recommended_dosage.churna: Not typically used as churna; 1-2 g dried leaf per cup
recommended_dosage.decoction: 150-200 ml light infusion; avoid long boiling of strong tea
recommended_dosage.extract: Use only as directed by a qualified practitioner

ayurvedic_properties.dosha_effect: May reduce Kapha in small amounts; excess readily aggravates Pitta and Vata because of heat, dryness and stimulation.

key_benefits.benefit: A light cup may support alertness and a feeling of clarity.
Bitter-astringent taste may feel reducing to excess Kapha after heavy food.
Used as a kitchen beverage, often with ginger, cardamom or milk according to local habit.

therapeutic_uses.use: Used as a mild after-meal drink when digestion feels heavy, in modest amounts.
Used as a household infusion; not a classical Kasahara herb like tulsi or ginger.
Sometimes combined with digestive spices in masala chai; milk and sugar change its effect and can increase Kapha.

safety_and_contraindications.safety: Contains caffeine. Excess may cause insomnia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor or acidity.
People with reflux, ulcers, marked Pitta, anxiety, insomnia, or Vata dryness should limit or avoid strong tea, especially on an empty stomach.
Tea tannins can reduce iron absorption; leave a gap around iron-rich meals or iron supplements if this is a concern.
Pregnant people, children, and those taking medicines (including for blood pressure, anxiety or sleep) should seek professional advice before using tea as a regular stimulant.
Do not confuse tea leaves with tulsi. For cough and congestion, tulsi or ginger infusions are the more traditional kitchen supports.
